title: What to keep from Montaigne
hook: curiosity, doubt, gentleness, laughter at ourselves

segments.voice: Yesterday, sleep and food: Montaigne says nature made our needs pleasant on purpose. Your line was ordinary pleasures. Which one did you actually taste? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-three.

Moving day. The truck is coming at nine, the boxes are full, and there's one small bag left for the things you won't let the movers touch. Not much fits. So you choose. We've spent weeks inside Montaigne's book, a big, rambling house of a book, with a room for nearly everything. Tomorrow we close the door on it. Today is the small bag. Four things seem worth carrying out: curiosity, doubt, gentleness, and laughter at ourselves. One by one.
screen: `ONE SMALL BAG.` → `A BIG, RAMBLING BOOK.` → `FOUR THINGS TO CARRY OUT.`

segments.voice: First, curiosity. Montaigne wanted to know how other people lived. He loved travel for the new and the different, and he turned the same curiosity on himself: his moods, his habits, his own changing mind. Nothing was too small to look at. Second, doubt. He took a question as a kind of motto: what do I know? Not as despair. As a brake. It kept him from being too sure, especially when being sure meant condemning someone. A man who doubts his own judgment is slower to burn a neighbor for a witch. Third, gentleness. He hated cruelty, and said so, even cruelty to animals. When he played with his cat, he wondered whether she was playing with him. That's a gentle mind: it leaves room for the other creature's point of view. Fourth, laughter at ourselves. On the highest throne in the world, he says, we still sit on our own bottom. He didn't laugh at other people's faith or other people's pain. He laughed at the human habit of taking ourselves too seriously, starting with his own. Notice how the four hold each other up. Curiosity without doubt turns into collecting opinions to win arguments. Doubt without gentleness turns cold. Gentleness without laughter gets heavy. And laughter without curiosity is just mockery. At the very end of his book, Montaigne asks not for a severe wisdom, but for a cheerful and sociable one. If only one thing fits in the bag, today's line picks curiosity, because it's the one that keeps the other three moving.
screen: `CURIOSITY: NOTHING TOO SMALL.` · `DOUBT: WHAT DO I KNOW?` · `GENTLENESS: ROOM FOR THE CAT.` · `LAUGHTER: STARTING WITH HIMSELF.` · then, large: `A CHEERFUL AND SOCIABLE WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one. Settle, and let the breath slow down. Say the four quietly: curiosity, doubt, gentleness, laughter. Notice which one tugs at you, maybe because you have it, maybe because you don't. Take that one. Now let a real moment from this week come to mind, a hard conversation, a quick judgment, a bad mood. Hold the quality you picked up to that moment, like a lamp. What would it have changed? Just look. The bell holds the time.
What to keep from Montaigne. Curiosity, doubt, gentleness, and laughter at ourselves, four habits that hold each other up. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT TO KEEP FROM MONTAIGNE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: keep curious. Today, when someone surprises or annoys you, ask one real question before you decide what you think of them. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Readers who spend time with Montaigne often come away keeping one habit rather than a doctrine, such as asking 'what do I know?' before judging, or laughing at their own self-importance.

original.note: Montaigne's French (in Latin letters): what do I know? The question he took as a kind of motto.
